numberItems.stem: About how long does it take an alert driver to perceive a hazard (from seeing it until the brain recognizes it)?
numberItems.explanation: The average perception time for an alert driver is 1¾ seconds; ¾ second to 1 second is the average reaction time (p. 2-15).

numberItems.stem: At 55 mph, how far does your vehicle travel during the average alert driver's perception time?
numberItems.explanation: 1¾ seconds of perception time at 55 mph accounts for 142 feet traveled (p. 2-15).

numberItems.stem: At 55 mph, about how far does the average driver travel during reaction time, before the brakes are applied?
numberItems.explanation: A reaction time of ¾ second to 1 second accounts for 61 feet at 55 mph (p. 2-15).

numberItems.stem: On dry pavement with good brakes, about how far does it take to brake to a stop from 55 mph (braking distance only)?
numberItems.explanation: Braking distance at 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes is about 216 feet (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: Add perception, reaction and braking distance at 55 mph in ideal conditions. What is the minimum total stopping distance?
numberItems.explanation: At 55 mph the total minimum stopping distance is 419 feet (142 + 61 + 216) (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: At 60 mph, how does your total stopping distance compare with an American football field?
options: It is longer than a football field
It is about half a football field
It is about 216 feet, well short of a football field
numberItems.explanation: At 60 mph, stopping distance is greater than the length of an American football field (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: Compared with driving at 20 mph, how much greater are the impact and braking distance at **80 mph**?
numberItems.explanation: Double the speed (20→40): 4 times; triple (20→60): 9 times; 80 mph: 16 times greater than at 20 mph (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: [CA] A single truck with a GVWR of 12,000 lb, not towing, must be able to stop from 20 mph within what maximum stopping distance?
numberItems.explanation: MSD from 20 mph: single vehicle with GVWR of 10,000 lb or more (or any bus) 40 ft; under 10,000 lb 30 ft; all other combinations 50 ft (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: The road is wet. By about how much should you reduce your speed?
options: By about one-third (for example, 55 to about 35 mph)
numberItems.explanation: Wet roads can double stopping distance; reduce speed by about ⅓, for example from 55 to about 35 mph (p. 2-16). Half or more is for packed snow.

numberItems.stem: The road surface is icy. What does the handbook tell you to do?
options: Reduce speed to a crawl and stop driving as soon as you can safely
numberItems.explanation: On an icy surface, reduce speed to a crawl and stop driving as soon as you can safely do so (p. 2-16).

numberItems.stem: If there is a lot of water on the road, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as:
numberItems.explanation: Hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water (p. 2-17).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Speed limits for trucks and buses are lower than for cars. By as much as how many mph can they differ?
numberItems.explanation: In California, truck and bus speed limits are lower than for cars and can vary by as much as 15 mph (p. 2-17).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Outside a business or residential district, a truck climbs a grade at 12 mph (under 20 mph). You may pass it only if you can:
options: Pass at least 10 mph faster and finish within 300 feet
Pass at least 10 mph faster and finish within ¼ mile
Pass at least 15 mph faster and finish within ¼ mile
numberItems.explanation: You may not pass a vehicle going under 20 mph on a grade unless you pass at least 10 mph faster and complete the pass within ¼ mile (CVC §21758, p. 2-18).

numberItems.stem: [CA] On a two-lane rural highway you are behind a 3-axle truck and are not passing. How far back must you stay?
numberItems.explanation: You must not follow the listed vehicles (such as trucks with 3 or more axles) closer than 300 feet, except when passing, on roads with 2+ lanes each way, or in business/residential districts (CVC §21704, p. 2-18).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Large vehicles driven in a caravan on the open highway must leave at least how much space between them?
numberItems.explanation: In a caravan, at least 100 feet must be left between large vehicles so others can pass (CVC §21705, p. 2-18). 300 feet is the following rule.

numberItems.stem: Fog and rain have cut your view. According to the handbook, you should always be able to stop within:
options: The distance you can see ahead
numberItems.explanation: You should always be able to stop within the distance you can see ahead; slow down in fog, rain or with low beams (p. 2-17).

numberItems.stem: If you take a curve too fast, what 2 things can happen?
options: The brakes overheat, or the engine over-revs
The tires lose traction and you skid off the road, or the tires keep traction and the vehicle rolls over
The trailer jackknifes, or the tires hydroplane
numberItems.explanation: Too fast in a curve: the tires can lose traction and skid off the road, or keep traction and the vehicle rolls over (p. 2-17).

numberItems.stem: What must be your principal way of controlling speed on a downgrade?
options: The braking effect of the engine, in a low gear
Steady pressure on the service brakes
numberItems.explanation: Use the braking effect of the engine as the principal way to control speed on downgrades; it is greatest near governed rpm in the lower gears (p. 2-18).
